title: NASA SCI Files - Volcano Eruptions
description:
NASA Why? Files segment describing volcanic activity and the Ring of Fire.

NASA Identifier: NasaSciFiles-VolcanoEruptions

transcript.text: Hi, you must be the tree house detectives.
And you are Dr. Peery?
I'm afraid so.
What's that plane behind you?
I've never seen anything like that before.
Well, it's an ER2. It's a NASA research aircraft used in high altitude.
What kind of research can NASA do at this point?
This plane has high-powered cameras, and they can see a wide variety of phenomenon.
We need hurricanes, volcanoes, earthquakes, and they can also monitor ozone.
You mean you actually fly into a volcano when it's erupting?
Oh, no. It would do a lot of damage to an airplane like this.
But how can this cause damage?
Well, this isn't so much a problem. This lava rock gets ground up into fine particular material like this.
This is volcanic ash. This is the problem.
That's really light. Where are most volcanoes located?
There are active volcanoes in every ocean basin, almost every continent in the world.
Most volcanoes are under water and form along ridges as ocean basins spread away from them.
Sometimes volcanoes form in the middle of continents and ocean basins, and it's hot spots heat up plates.
Plates?
The Earth's crust is actually broken into pieces that we call plates.
In fact, another place where volcanoes form is where one plate goes underneath another plate, and that happens in the Pacific Ocean.
Are you talking about the Ring of Fire?
The Ring of Fire is a ring of volcanoes that surround the Pacific Ocean where the continents meet the ocean basin.
We learned that Mount Loomis is a cinder cone. Could you tell us more about cinder cones?
Well sure. For instance, when cinder cones form, the magma so sticky that the gas stays trapped inside it until the pressure builds so much that it just literally explodes.
When it explodes, it forms lots of pyroclastic material, which is really sharp.
Maybe we're getting a little closer.
Thanks, Dr. Perry. We learned so much about volcanoes.
Well, I hope this information gives you your answer.
Thank you so much.
Good luck.
Bye.
Bye-bye.
